title: Vintage Calculator Tape
story: An old office calculator has no = key and no brackets. You type a number, press Enter, type another, and then press an operator, which combines the two most recent numbers into one. To work out (2 + 1) × 3 you type 2, 1, +, 3, *.
The calculator prints every key on a paper tape. A shop found a box of old tapes, and wants to know the final number each one produced.
task: Write replayTape(tokens). tokens is the tape: each entry is either an integer written as a string (it may be negative, like "-5") or one of the operators "+", "-", "*", "/". An operator takes the two most recent numbers, a (older) and b (newer), and replaces them with a op b. Return the one number left at the end.
Division keeps only the whole part and rounds toward zero: 7 / 2 is 3 and -7 / 2 is -3.
constraints: Every tape is valid: an operator always has two numbers to use, and exactly one number is left at the end.
No division by zero. Every number, including intermediate results, is between -2,147,483,648 and 2,147,483,647.

examples.explanation: 2 and 1 are typed. + combines them into 3. Then 3 is typed, and * combines the two numbers waiting, 3 and 3, into 9.
4, 13 and 5 wait. / combines the two newest: 13 / 5 = 2.6, cut to 2. Now 4 and 2 wait, and + gives 6. The 4 waited the whole time for its partner.

hints: In ["4", "13", "5", "/", "+"], the / uses 13 and 5, not 4. Which numbers does an operator always use?
An operator always takes the two numbers typed or produced most recently. The result then becomes the newest number, ready for the next operator.
"The most recent one comes out first" is the rule of a stack. Also mind the order: the first number you pop is b, the right-hand side.

Walk the tokens. Push numbers. On an operator, pop b, then pop a, push a op b. For division, truncate toward zero (Math.trunc in JavaScript, int(a / b) in Python). The answer is the last number on the stack.
bruteForce: Scan the tape for the first spot where two numbers are followed by an operator, replace those three tokens with the result, and start the scan again. Repeat until one number is left.

Each scan finds one operation and the list shrinks by only two tokens, so a tape of 10,000 tokens needs about 5,000 scans of up to 10,000 tokens each, around 50 million steps. A stack does the whole tape in one pass.

js: * @param {string[]} tokens  numbers and + - * / keys, in order

tests.note: a single number, no keys pressed
a negative number token is not a minus key
four numbers wait on the stack
negative numbers mixed with minus keys
truncation inside a longer tape: rounding down would give -8

js: const b = nums.pop(); // newest number is the right-hand side
else nums.push(Math.trunc(a / b)); // round toward zero
py: b = nums.pop()  # newest number is the right-hand side
nums.append(int(a / b))  # round toward zero, unlike //
walkthrough: Numbers wait until an operator arrives, and the operator always takes the newest two. That is a stack: push numbers, and let each operator pop two and push one.
• /: pop b = 5, pop a = 13. 13 / 5 = 2.6, truncated to 2. Push it. Stack: [4, 2].
• +: pop b = 2, pop a = 4. Push 6. Stack: [6].
The tape is over and one number is left: 6.

Two traps. First, pop order: the first pop is the right operand, so 3 10 - is 3 - 10 = -7. Second, Python's // rounds down, so -7 // 2 is -4; the task wants -3, which int(-7 / 2) gives. Also check for operators by exact match, so a token like "-5" is read as a number.
solution.timeWhy: Each token is pushed or causes two pops and one push, all O(1).
solution.spaceWhy: A tape of many numbers before any operator puts them all on the stack.
solution.takeaway: Postfix expressions need no brackets because a stack remembers the waiting operands. The same push-operands, pop-on-operator loop is how many interpreters and calculators evaluate expressions once they are parsed.
